Q1.answer:
The section 338 Canada series through Nov. 14, 2026 consists of ten presidential documents:

1. **Proclamation 11046**, FR Doc. 2026-14991, 91 FR 46639, signed July 20, 2026, published July 23, 2026. Imposes a 50% section 338 duty on the Canadian alcoholic-beverage products in Annex II. Operative date: 12:01 a.m. ET Aug. 19, 2026, measured against goods **entered for consumption or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption**; later changed to Aug. 22, 2026 by Proclamation 11056.
2. **Proclamation 11047**, FR Doc. 2026-14992, 91 FR 46653, signed July 20, 2026, published July 23, 2026. Imposes 50% on the Canadian dairy products in Annex II. Same Aug. 19 entry/withdrawal date, later changed to Aug. 22.
3. **Proclamation 11048**, FR Doc. 2026-14997, 91 FR 46663, signed July 20, 2026, published July 23, 2026. Imposes 50% on the Canadian motor-vehicle products in Annex II. Same Aug. 19 entry/withdrawal date, later changed to Aug. 22.
4. **Proclamation 11056**, FR Doc. 2026-17294, 91 FR 54789, signed Aug. 18, 2026, published Aug. 24, 2026. Changes the effective date of all three original duties to 12:01 a.m. ET Aug. 22, 2026. The change is measured against goods entered for consumption or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption.
5. **Proclamation 11061**, FR Doc. 2026-18835, 91 FR 58311, signed Sept. 8, 2026, published Sept. 14, 2026. Excludes the Canadian alcoholic-beverage products in its Annex from importation. Operative date: 12:01 a.m. ET Sept. 29, 2026, measured against goods **imported** on or after that time (not entry for consumption).
6. **Proclamation 11062**, FR Doc. 2026-18836, 91 FR 58319, signed Sept. 8, 2026, published Sept. 14, 2026. Excludes the Canadian dairy products in its Annex from importation, also measured against goods imported on or after 12:01 a.m. ET Sept. 29, 2026.
7. **Proclamation 11063**, FR Doc. 2026-18837, 91 FR 58325, signed Sept. 8, 2026, published Sept. 14, 2026. Excludes the Canadian motor-vehicle products in its Annex from importation, measured against goods imported on or after 12:01 a.m. ET Sept. 29, 2026.
8. **Proclamation 11064**, FR Doc. 2026-18838, 91 FR 58331, signed Sept. 8, 2026, published Sept. 14, 2026. Modifies the alcoholic-beverage duty scope: Annex I, Part A products become subject to the 50% duty; Annex I, Part B products cease to be subject. Effective 12:01 a.m. ET Sept. 15, 2026, measured against entry for consumption or withdrawal from warehouse for consumption.
9. **Proclamation 11065**, FR Doc. 2026-18839, 91 FR 58339, signed Sept. 8, 2026, published Sept. 14, 2026. Modifies the motor-vehicle duty scope: Annex I, Part A products become subject; Annex I, Part B products cease to be subject. Effective 12:01 a.m. ET Sept. 15, 2026, measured against entry/withdrawal for consumption.
10. **Proclamation 11076**, FR Doc. 2026-22292, 91 FR 68861, signed Oct. 23, 2026, published Oct. 30, 2026. Further modifies the motor-vehicle duty scope: Annex I, Part A products cease to be subject; Annex I, Part B products become subject. Effective 12:01 a.m. ET Oct. 30, 2026, measured against entry/withdrawal for consumption.

**Product-group changes:**
- **Alcoholic beverages:** 11046 imposed the duty on Annex II; 11056 delayed it; 11064 added Part A and removed Part B products; 11061 replaced the duty with an import ban for its Annex products beginning Sept. 29, 2026.
- **Dairy:** 11047 imposed the duty on Annex II; 11056 delayed it; 11062 replaced the duty with an import ban for its Annex products beginning Sept. 29, 2026. No dairy scope-modification proclamation was published, despite 11062's reference to one.
- **Motor vehicles:** 11048 imposed the duty on Annex II; 11056 delayed it; 11065 added Part A and removed Part B products effective Sept. 15, 2026; 11063 banned its Annex products from importation effective Sept. 29, 2026; 11076 removed Part A and added Part B products effective Oct. 30, 2026.
Q1.uncertainty: The annexes are images, so the product lists themselves cannot be read in the text. The descriptions above identify the legal effect of each Annex/Part, not the tariff lines within them. No dairy scope-modification proclamation appears in the Federal Register through Nov. 14, 2026.

Q2.answer:
(a) Entry 1 (Aug. 20, 2:00 p.m.): **$0**. Entry 2 (Aug. 21, 11:59 p.m.): **$0**. Entry 3 (Aug. 22, 12:01 a.m.): **$20,000**. The duty is 50% of $40,000 = $20,000. The controlling effective time is 12:01 a.m. ET Aug. 22, 2026, so entry 3 is the first entry on or after the effective time.

(b) Proclamation 11056 changed the date from Aug. 19 to Aug. 22. Its clause (1) says the effective date of the duties in Proclamations 11046, 11047 and 11048 "shall be 12:01 a.m. eastern time on August 22, 2026," and it amended **only the chapeau of Annex II** of each proclamation by replacing "August 19, 2026" with "August 22, 2026." It did **not** amend the operative clauses (1) and (3) in the body of the original proclamations, which still read Aug. 19. The difference is resolved by 11056 clause (1)'s direct statement that the effective date "shall be" Aug. 22, by 11056 clause (5) (superseding inconsistent provisions), and by the later proclamations, which state that at 12:01 a.m. ET Aug. 22 the suspension lapsed and the duties became effective (e.g., 11061 paras. 3-4; 11062 paras. 3-4; 11063 paras. 3-4; 11064 paras. 3-4; 11065 paras. 3-4; 11076 paras. 3-4).

(c) Entry 1 was before the effective date, so the $20,000 deposited as 50% duty was not owed. Proclamation 11056 clause (4) says that, to the extent implementation requires a refund, "refunds shall be processed pursuant to applicable law and CBP's standard procedures for such refunds." The documents do not prescribe a special refund form or deadline.

(d) No further presidential action was required for the duties to begin. The suspension fixed a new date, and the later documents state that Canada reneged on Aug. 21, 2026, that the 3-day suspension lapsed at 12:01 a.m. ET Aug. 22, and that the duties became effective at that time. See 11061 paras. 3-4, 91 FR 58311.

(e) The original start date was 30 days after the July 20, 2026 signing. Counting July 21 as day 1, Aug. 19 is day 30; equivalently, July 20 + 30 calendar days = Aug. 19, 2026. Section 338 and the proclamation's finding required that the duty not take effect earlier than 30 days after the proclamation finding. See 11046 para. 10 and cl. (1), 91 FR 46640.
Q2.basis: Proclamation 11046, 91 FR 46639, para. 9 and cl. (1), 91 FR 46640; Proclamation 11056, 91 FR 54789, cl. (1) and (4), 91 FR 54790-91; Proclamation 11061, 91 FR 58311, paras. 1-4, 91 FR 58311-12; parallel paragraphs in 11062, 11063, 11064, 11065 and 11076. For the 30-day arithmetic: 11046 para. 10, 91 FR 46640.
Q2.uncertainty: The original operative clauses (1) and (3) of 11046/11047/11048 were not conformed and still print Aug. 19. A broker should rely on 11056 clause (1), the superseding clause, and the later confirming proclamations, but the internal inconsistency is real.

Q3.answer:
(a) A. Arrives Sept. 10, entered Sept. 14: **may be imported; $15,000 section 338 duty** (50% × $30,000). The beer is in Annex II, was not removed by the scope modification, and entry occurred before the Sept. 29 import ban.

B. Arrives Sept. 27, bonded warehouse, withdrawn Oct. 5: **may be entered; $15,000 section 338 duty**. It was imported before Sept. 29 but not entered/withdrawn before that date; 11061 cl. (2) preserves the 50% duty rate for such goods.

C. Arrives 11:30 p.m. Sept. 28, entry 9:00 a.m. Sept. 29: **$15,000 section 338 duty**. Same reason: imported before Sept. 29, not yet entered; cl. (2) preserves the 50% duty.

D. Arrives 12:30 a.m. Sept. 29, wants to enter that morning: **the import ban applies; the beer may not be imported/entered for consumption, and no section 338 duty is assessed because entry is prohibited**. It was imported on Sept. 29, on or after the effective time of 11061.

(b) E arrives Sept. 25 and is admitted to an FTZ that day; entered for consumption Oct. 6. On the best reading of the text, **the 50% duty applies ($15,000), not the ban**, because it was imported before Sept. 29 but not entered for consumption. It was required to be admitted in privileged foreign status under 11046 cl. (4), and 11061 cl. (2) preserves the 50% rate for goods imported but not entered before Sept. 29. The text does not expressly define whether FTZ admission counts as "imported"; if it does not, the ban would apply instead. The more defensible reading, given cl. (2)'s purpose, is that the duty is preserved and the goods must be entered under privileged foreign status.

(c) If a court invalidates the import ban as applied to this beer, **the 50% section 338 duty applies to later imports of that beer** under 11061 cl. (9)(b), which says the 50% duty in Proclamation 11046 "shall apply to the import to which the invalidated import ban ... had applied before its invalidation." No new proclamation is required by the text.

(d) No. The exclusion proclamation does not change the duty on listed Canadian alcoholic products that are not in its Annex. 11061 cl. (3) says that, besides changing the listed products from duty to import ban, the proclamation "does not otherwise affect" the products subject to the duties established by the September 8 scope modification. Those products remain subject to the 50% duty under 11046 as modified by 11064.
Q3.basis: Proclamation 11046 cl. (1), (4), 91 FR 46640; Proclamation 11061 cl. (1)-(3) and (9)(b), 91 FR 58312-13; Proclamation 11064 cl. (1), 91 FR 58332.
Q3.uncertainty: The FTZ point in (b): the documents do not define "imported" for FTZ admission. If CBP treats FTZ admission as outside the customs territory and not an importation, the Sept. 29 ban would apply on the Oct. 6 entry. The text is silent on that specific question.

Q4.answer:
(a) Entries Sept. 10, 2026:
- X: section 232 **$25,000**; section 338 **$0**.
- Y: section 232 **$25,000**; section 338 **$0**.
- Z: section 232 **$25,000**; section 338 **$0**.

All three original section 338 proclamations were in effect by Aug. 22, but each provided that the section 338 duty "shall not apply to articles subject to duties pursuant to section 232." 91 FR 46640 (alcohol), 46654 (dairy), 46664 (motor vehicles).

(b) Entries Oct. 1, 2026:
- X: section 232 **$25,000**; section 338 **$50,000**.
- Y: section 232 **$25,000**; section 338 **$0**.
- Z: section 232 **$25,000**; section 338 **$50,000**.

The alcohol and motor-vehicle scope modifications, effective Sept. 15, 2026, state: "The duties imposed pursuant to Proclamation 11046 [or 11048], as modified in this proclamation, shall apply in addition to duties imposed pursuant to section 232." 91 FR 58332; 91 FR 58340. X and Z are therefore stacked. Y is dairy; no dairy scope modification was published, so the original dairy clause (2) exclusion of section 232 articles still governs.
Q4.basis: Proclamation 11046 cl. (2), 91 FR 46640; Proclamation 11047 cl. (2), 91 FR 46654; Proclamation 11048 cl. (2), 91 FR 46664; Proclamation 11064 cl. (1), 91 FR 58332; Proclamation 11065 cl. (1), 91 FR 58340.
Q4.uncertainty: The scope-modification sentence does not expressly say it amends the original clause (2) for products that are not in Annex I, Part A or B. The better reading is that it makes the remaining 11046/11048 duties stack with section 232 generally; if read narrowly, X and Z would remain excluded because they are not in Part A. The later text and the evident purpose support stacking.

Q5.answer:
(a) P: Sept. 14, 3:00 p.m. **No**; Sept. 15, 12:01 a.m. **Yes**; Oct. 29, 4:00 p.m. **Yes**; Oct. 30, 12:01 a.m. **Yes**; Nov. 3 **Yes**. P was newly added by the September Part A and was not removed in October.

Q: Sept. 14, 3:00 p.m. **Yes** (original Annex II); Sept. 15, 12:01 a.m. **No** (September Part B removal); Oct. 29, 4:00 p.m. **No**; Oct. 30, 12:01 a.m. **No**; Nov. 3 **No**.

R: Sept. 14, 3:00 p.m. **Yes**; Sept. 15, 12:01 a.m. **Yes**; Oct. 29, 4:00 p.m. **Yes**; Oct. 30, 12:01 a.m. **No** (October Part A removal); Nov. 3 **No**.

S: Sept. 14, 3:00 p.m. **No**; Sept. 15, 12:01 a.m. **No**; Oct. 29, 4:00 p.m. **No**; Oct. 30, 12:01 a.m. **Yes** (October Part B addition); Nov. 3 **Yes**.

(b) Proclamation 11076 was signed Oct. 23, 2026; filed with the Office of the Federal Register Oct. 29, 2026 at 11:15 a.m. (FR Doc. filing line); published Oct. 30, 2026; and applies to goods entered for consumption or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption on or after 12:01 a.m. ET Oct. 30, 2026. It does not reach entries made before that time; its text contains no refund provision for pre-effective-date entries.

(c) P became dutiable on Sept. 15, 2026, seven days after the Sept. 8 signing. S became dutiable on Oct. 30, 2026, seven days after the Oct. 23 signing. As to the section 338 30-day waiting period, the scope proclamations recite that a duty may not take effect earlier than 30 days after the President's proclamation finding, but they do not explain how a seven-day implementation fits. The best explanation in the documents is that the finding was made in the original July 20 proclamations; Sept. 15 was 57 days after July 20, and Oct. 30 was 102 days after July 20. The scope proclamations themselves do not spell this out.
Q5.basis: Proclamation 11065 cl. (1), 91 FR 58339-40; Proclamation 11076 cl. (1), 91 FR 68862 and FR Doc. filing line, 91 FR 68871; original findings, Proclamation 11046 para. 10, 91 FR 46640, and 11048 para. 9, 91 FR 46664.
Q5.uncertainty: The documents do not expressly reconcile the scope proclamations' seven-day implementation with the quoted 30-day rule. The explanation based on the original July 20 finding is an inference from the text, not an express statement.

Q6.answer:
(a) Section 301 duty on $100,000; then MFN $4,000 plus section 301:
1. Switzerland: 12.5% net of MFN; 12.5% − 4% = **8.5% = $8,500**; total **$12,500**.
2. Norway: **12.5% = $12,500**; total **$16,500**.
3. United Kingdom: **10% = $10,000**; total **$14,000**.
4. Germany (EU): 10% net of MFN; 10% − 4% = **6% = $6,000**; total **$10,000**.
5. Taiwan: 10% net of MFN; 10% − 4% = **6% = $6,000**; total **$10,000**.
6. Türkiye: **12.5% = $12,500**; total **$16,500**.
7. Japan: 12.5% net of MFN; 12.5% − 4% = **8.5% = $8,500**; total **$12,500**.
8. Liechtenstein: not one of the 60 investigated economies; **$0**; total **$4,000**.
9. Hong Kong: **12.5% = $12,500**; total **$16,500**.
10. India: **10% = $10,000**; total **$14,000**.

(b) Section 301 only:
- Germany, MFN 12%: EU net 10%; because MFN is at least 10%, **$0**.
- Japan, MFN 12%: net 12.5%; 12.5% − 12% = 0.5% × $100,000 = **$500**.
- Taiwan, MFN exactly 10%: at or above the 10% cap, **$0**.
- South Korea, MFN exactly 10%: net 12.5%; 12.5% − 10% = 2.5% × $100,000 = **$2,500**.
- Switzerland, MFN free: **12.5% = $12,500**.

(c) Compared with the June 2026 proposal: the June proposal used flat rates and did not use net-of-MFN rates. The adopted treatment differs for:
- **Germany/EU:** June 10% flat; adopted 10% net of MFN.
- **Taiwan:** June 10% flat; adopted 10% net of MFN.
- **Japan:** June 12.5% flat; adopted 12.5% net of MFN.
- **Switzerland:** June 12.5% flat; adopted 12.5% net of MFN.
- **India:** June 12.5% flat; adopted **10% flat**. The notice states that India adopted a forced-labor import prohibition after the June 5 notice; that is the stated reason for the 10% rate. 91 FR 47319, 47324.
- **Norway, United Kingdom, Türkiye, Hong Kong:** no change in the nominal rate. Liechtenstein was not investigated.
Q6.basis: Proclamation/memorandum: 91 FR 47717, §1(a), 91 FR 47720. Notice: 91 FR 47318-28, especially EU at 47323, Japan at 47324, South Korea at 47327, Switzerland at 47327, Taiwan at 47327-28, UK at 47328, Türkiye at 47327-28, India at 47324, Norway at 47326, Hong Kong at 47324. June proposal: 91 FR 34272, 34274.
Q6.uncertainty: These amounts assume the product is not exempt under Annex I or Annex II. The annex product lists are images; if the particular article is listed, the section 301 duty would be zero or different.

Q7.answer:
(a) France (EU), 3 cents/kg, 2,000 kg, value $12,000:
- Column 1 duty = $0.03 × 2,000 = **$60**.
- Ad valorem equivalent = $60 ÷ $12,000 = **0.5%**.
- EU net-of-MFN cap = 10%; section 301 rate = 10% − 0.5% = **9.5%**.
- Section 301 duty = 9.5% × $12,000 = **$1,140**.

(b) 4% plus 25 cents/kg; 4,000 kg; value $20,000:
- Column 1 duty = (4% × $20,000) + ($0.25 × 4,000) = $800 + $1,000 = **$1,800**.
- Ad valorem equivalent = $1,800 ÷ $20,000 = **9%**.
- **Italy (EU):** 10% − 9% = 1% × $20,000 = **$200**.
- **Japan:** 12.5% − 9% = 3.5% × $20,000 = **$700**.
- **Brazil:** flat 12.5% × $20,000 = **$2,500**.

(c) MFN duty $2,200 on $20,000 = **11%**:
- **Taiwan:** 10% net; MFN is at least 10%, so section 301 = **$0**.
- **Switzerland:** 12.5% net; 12.5% − 11% = 1.5% × $20,000 = **$300**.

(d) The rule is U.S. note 52(k) to the HTSUS, 91 FR 47394: for a good of an EU member state, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland or Taiwan subject to a specific or compound Column 1-General rate, the ad valorem equivalent is the amount of Column 1 duty divided by the customs value. The same page states the cap result: for headings 9903.05.39 and 9903.05.76 (10% net), if the Column 1 rate is less than 10%, the sum is 10%; for headings 9903.05.49, 9903.05.71 and 9903.05.74 (12.5% net), if the Column 1 rate is less than 12.5%, the sum is 12.5%. If the Column 1 rate is at or above the cap, the section 301 rate is zero.
Q7.basis: Notice, U.S. note 52(k), 91 FR 47394; rate provisions, 91 FR 47320-21 and country determinations at 47323-28.
Q7.uncertainty: None, assuming the goods are not exempt under Annex I or Annex II.

Q8.answer:
(a) Dominican Republic rate: 12.5% flat; each value $80,000, so full duty = **$10,000**.
1. Loaded July 22, entered July 29: **$10,000**. The transit exception requires entry before July 28; July 29 is too late.
2. Same sailing, entered July 27 at 3:00 p.m.: **$0**. Loaded before July 24 and entered before July 28.
3. Same sailing, entered July 28 at 12:01 a.m.: **$10,000**. The exception requires entry **before** 12:01 a.m. July 28; 12:01 is not before.
4. Loaded July 24 at 6:00 a.m., entered July 27: **$10,000**. The goods were not loaded before 12:01 a.m. July 24.
5. Entered July 23: **$0**. Before the July 24 effective time.
6. In bonded warehouse since June, withdrawn July 26: **$10,000**. The transit exception applies to goods loaded onto a vessel and in transit before July 24; warehouse goods were not in transit, so the July 24 duty applies on withdrawal.
7. Air freight loaded July 23 at 9:00 p.m., entered July 25: **$10,000**. The exception is limited to goods loaded onto a **vessel**; air freight does not qualify.

(b) The rule is in the DATES line of the notice, 91 FR 47318: goods "loaded onto a vessel at the port of loading and in transit on the final mode of transit before 12:01 a.m. eastern time on July 24, 2026, and entered for consumption or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption before 12:01 a.m. eastern time on July 28, 2026" are not subject to the additional duty.

(c) Signed July 23, 2026; effective 12:01 a.m. ET July 24, 2026; published July 28, 2026.

(d) Heading 9903.04.62 is within the patented-pharmaceutical exemption added effective July 31, 2026. Entered July 30: **$10,000** (12.5% × $80,000), because the exemption was not yet effective. Entered Aug. 3: **$0**.
Q8.basis: Notice DATES line, 91 FR 47318; Dominican Republic determination, 91 FR 47323; Annex I note 2.B, 91 FR 47394 (effective July 31, 2026, adding patented pharmaceutical articles and note 52(f)(8), headings 9903.04.60-9903.04.66).
Q8.uncertainty: None on the dates given, assuming the goods are not otherwise exempt under Annex I or Annex II.

Q9.answer:
(a) Thailand, 9802.00.80: the section 301 duty applies to the value of the article assembled abroad less the cost or value of U.S. products. $100,000 − $35,000 = $65,000. Thailand rate 12.5% × $65,000 = **$8,125**.

(b) Israel, 9802.00.50: the duty applies to the value of repairs/alterations/processing. $6,000 × 12.5% = **$750**.

(c) Mexico, value $50,000:
(i) USMCA claim: **$0** section 301 duty. Heading 9903.05.94 exempts Mexican products entered free of duty under USMCA.
(ii) No USMCA claim: Mexico rate 10% × $50,000 = **$5,000** section 301 duty.

(d) Japanese passenger car under section 232 heading 9903.94.01: **$0** section 301 duty. Note 52(f)(2) exempts passenger vehicles provided for in heading 9903.94.01.

(e) Brazil, value $100,000, section 232 duty under a chapter 99 heading not mentioned in the section 301 note: **$12,500** section 301 duty. The adopted section 301 exemption is not a general exemption for all section 232 goods; it lists specific headings in note 52(f). Because the Brazilian heading is not listed, the 12.5% Brazil rate applies.

(f) June proposal: it stated that the proposed action did not cover informational materials, donations, accompanied baggage, and **all articles and parts of articles subject to section 232 tariffs**. 91 FR 34276. Adopted text: the section 232 exemption is limited to the specific headings listed in note 52(f), 91 FR 47362-63; informational materials and donations are **not** stated as exemptions in the operative text; only accompanied baggage for personal use is preserved in note 52(a), 91 FR 47352. The preamble at 91 FR 47318 accurately describes what the June proposal contained, but the adopted operative text does not carry forward a general informational-materials or donations exemption or an all-section-232 exemption.
Q9.basis: Note 52(a), 91 FR 47352; note 52(f), 91 FR 47362-63; Mexico and Brazil determinations, 91 FR 47323, 47325; June proposal Annex A note, 91 FR 34276; adopted notice preamble, 91 FR 47318 and 47334.
Q9.uncertainty: The adopted Annex I and Annex II product lists are images, so a particular informational material or donated article could still be covered by an Annex product exemption. The text does not contain a general exemption for those categories.

Q10.answer:
Scenario 1 (aluminum extrusions; value $200,000; MFN 3% = $6,000):
(a) Sept. 10, 2026: MFN **$6,000**; section 232 **$100,000** (50%); section 338 **$0** (the original motor-vehicle clause (2) excludes section 232 articles and the Sept. 15 stacking change was not yet effective); section 301 **$0** (note 52(f)(1) exempts aluminum articles under heading 9903.82.02). **Total $106,000**.
(b) Sept. 16, 2026: MFN **$6,000**; section 232 **$100,000**; section 338 **$100,000** (the Sept. 15 motor-vehicle scope modification makes the 338 duty apply in addition to section 232); section 301 **$0**. **Total $206,000**.

Scenario 2 (rye whisky; value $60,000; MFN free):
(c) Sept. 1, 2026, USMCA claim: section 338 **$30,000**; section 301 **$0** (heading 9903.05.93 exempts Canadian goods entered free under USMCA). **Total $30,000**.
(d) Sept. 1, 2026, no USMCA claim: section 338 **$30,000**; section 301 **$6,000** (Canada 10%); **total $36,000**.
(e) Arrives Oct. 2, 2026: the whisky is in the Annex to Proclamation 11061 and is **excluded from importation** effective Sept. 29, 2026. It may not be entered for consumption; no lawful duty total arises. If it had been imported before Sept. 29 but not entered, 11061 cl. (2) would preserve the 50% duty.

(f) No. The IEEPA northern-border duties were imposed by EO 14193 (Feb. 1, 2025), as amended, but EO 14389 (Feb. 20, 2026) ended the additional ad valorem duties imposed under IEEPA, including those in EO 14193, and directed that they no longer be collected. 91 FR 9437-38. The 10% temporary import surcharge under Proclamation 11012 ran for 150 days, effective Feb. 24, 2026 and through 12:01 a.m. EDT July 24, 2026. 91 FR 9341, 9343. It was also inapplicable to section 232 articles and USMCA-duty-free Canadian goods. Thus Canadian goods entered in September 2026 bear neither the IEEPA northern-border duty nor the temporary surcharge.
Q10.basis: Section 232: Proclamation 11021 cl. (2), 91 FR 18203-04; section 338: Proclamation 11048 cl. (2), 91 FR 46664; Proclamation 11065 cl. (1), 91 FR 58340; section 301: note 52(f)(1), 91 FR 47362; USMCA: note 52(g), 91 FR 47363; exclusion: Proclamation 11061 cl. (1)-(2), 91 FR 58312; IEEPA termination: EO 14389, 91 FR 9437-38; surcharge: Proclamation 11012 paras. 13, 17 and cls. (2), (4), (7), 91 FR 9341-43.
Q10.uncertainty: The whisky's Oct. 2 status assumes it is within the Annex to 11061, as the scenario states. The annex is an image, so the specific product line cannot be checked from the text.

Q11.answer:
The principal discrepancies I find are:

1. **The Aug. 19/Aug. 22 conflict.** Proclamation 11056 cl. (1) says the effective date "shall be 12:01 a.m. eastern time on August 22, 2026" and amends only the Annex II chapeau of 11046/11047/11048. But the operative clauses (1) and (3) of each original proclamation still say Aug. 19. Later proclamations repeat both dates: e.g., 11061 para. 1 says the duties were "effective August 19, 2026," while para. 4 says they "became effective" at 12:01 a.m. Aug. 22. 91 FR 58311. The same pattern appears in 11062 at 58319, 11063 at 58325, 11064 at 58331, 11065 at 58339 and 11076 at 68861.

2. **Only the annex chapeau was amended.** 11056 cl. (1) expressly amends "the chapeau of Annex II" and does not amend the body clauses. 91 FR 54790. The body clauses therefore continue to print Aug. 19, creating an internal conflict with the new annex date.

3. **The missing dairy scope proclamation.** Proclamation 11062 cl. (3) refers to "the Proclamation of September 8, 2026 (Modifying the Scope of Products of Canada Subject to the Additional Duties ... With Respect to Dairy)." 91 FR 58320. No such dairy scope-modification proclamation appears in the Federal Register through Nov. 14, 2026. The alcohol and motor-vehicle scope modifications exist (11064 and 11065), but the dairy one does not.

4. **Section 232 stacking conflict.** The original alcohol, dairy and motor-vehicle proclamations say the section 338 duties "shall not apply to articles subject to duties pursuant to section 232." 91 FR 46640, 46654, 46664. The September alcohol and motor-vehicle scope modifications say the duties "as modified" "shall apply in addition to duties imposed pursuant to section 232." 91 FR 58332, 58340. The later text does not expressly amend the original clause (2); it simply conflicts with it for products remaining in scope.

5. **The June proposal's textile rate.** The July 23 memorandum says the Trade Representative proposed a textile mechanism allowing apparel/textiles to enter "at a zero section 301 tariff rate." 91 FR 47719. The June 5 proposal actually says a "reduced Section 301 tariff rate," not a zero rate. 91 FR 34272, 34274. The adopted notice says the TRQ mechanism will allow goods to enter "free of the section 301 tariffs," 91 FR 47334, so the memorandum describes the proposal in terms of the later adopted design rather than the proposal's text.

6. **The "maximum 12.5 percent" statement.** The notice says commenters failed to show economy-wide disruptions "particularly with maximum tariffs of 12.5 percent." 91 FR 47334. Operatively, 12.5% is the maximum **section 301 additional** rate; for flat-rate economies it is added to MFN, so total duties can exceed 12.5%. Only the EU/Taiwan and Japan/Korea/Switzerland net-rate groups are capped at a 10% or 12.5% total. 91 FR 47320-21.

7. **The June proposal's 450 comments/nearly 60 witnesses versus the adopted action's 1,600 comments/over 100 witnesses.** The June 5 proposal describes the earlier March-initiation comment round as "over 450 written comments" and "nearly 60 witnesses." 91 FR 34273. The July notice and memorandum describe the June proposal round as "over 1,600 written comments" and "over 100 witnesses." 91 FR 47319; 91 FR 47719. Each statement is accurate for its own round; the discrepancy arises only if one document is read as describing the other round.
Q11.basis: Citations given in each numbered item.
Q11.uncertainty: The annexes are images, so I cannot check whether any Annex list itself contains a cross-reference or product description that resolves items 3 or 4. Item 7 is a discrepancy only as a matter of which comment round is being described; the two documents are internally accurate about their respective rounds.

Q13.answer:
All values $200,000. The machine is in Annex I-C of the June 2026 proclamation, so the temporary Annex I-C rate through Dec. 31, 2027 is 25% generally, with the Canada/Mexico USMCA rule of 25% on non-U.S. content subject to a 15% minimum, and a 10% rate only if the metal content is entirely U.S. (at least 85% by weight).

(a) Canada, USMCA claim, $60,000 U.S. parts: non-U.S. content = $140,000; 25% × $140,000 = $35,000. Minimum 15% × $200,000 = $30,000; $35,000 exceeds the floor. **$35,000**.
(b) Canada, USMCA, no U.S. content: 25% × $200,000 = $50,000. **$50,000**.
(c) Canada, no USMCA claim: general 25% × $200,000 = $50,000. **$50,000**.
(d) Japan, MFN 2.5%: Japan is in the clause (2)(b) group. Sum of Column 1 rate and section 232 rate must be 15%; section 232 = 15% − 2.5% = 12.5% × $200,000 = **$25,000**.
(e) Canada, USMCA, $20,000 U.S. parts plus $30,000 U.S.-smelted aluminum in a Canadian part: the $30,000 is not a "part produced in the United States"; the metal content is not entirely U.S. Non-U.S. content = $180,000; 25% × $180,000 = $45,000, above the $30,000 floor. **$45,000**.
(f) Same as (e), entered Oct. 6, 2026: the Annex I-C rate still applies; **$45,000**.
(g) Canada, USMCA, $140,000 U.S. parts: non-U.S. content = $60,000; 25% × $60,000 = $15,000, but the 15% floor is $30,000. **$30,000**.
(h) The treatment in (a) applies through 11:59 p.m. EST Dec. 31, 2027. From Jan. 1, 2028, the rate is the rate set out in clause (3) of Proclamation 11021: 25%, or 10% only if the metal content is entirely U.S. Because this machine's metal is mostly foreign, the rate would be 25% of the full customs value = **$50,000**.
Q13.basis: Proclamation 11032 cl. (2), (3), (4), 91 FR 34087-88; Proclamation 11021 cl. (3), 91 FR 18204.
Q13.uncertainty: The 85%-by-weight rule in clause (4) is satisfied only if U.S. aluminum/steel/copper is at least 85% of the metal weight. The scenario says most metal was melted or smelted outside the U.S., so the 10% rate is unavailable.

Q14.answer:
1. **Incorrect.** The memorandum does not give USTR a Sept. 1, 2026 deadline. It says establishing the TRQs is not feasible at this time but will be feasible by Sept. 1, 2026, and directs USTR to establish them "as soon as" it determines feasibility. 91 FR 47719-20, 47720-21.
2. **Incorrect as a description of the June proposal round.** The June 5 proposal says USTR received over 450 comments and heard nearly 60 witnesses in the earlier round on the March initiation. 91 FR 34273. The July notice and memorandum say the June proposal round produced over 1,600 written comments and over 100 witnesses. 91 FR 47319; 91 FR 47719.
3. **Partly correct / materially inaccurate.** The June proposal already gave 10% to Cambodia and Guatemala as ART economies. 91 FR 34274. After June, six economies adopted forced-labor import bans (Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago), and Jordan undertook an ART commitment. 91 FR 47319. But only Honduras, India, Sri Lanka and Trinidad and Tobago moved from 12.5% to 10% because of a ban; Jordan moved because of its ART; Cambodia and Guatemala were already at 10%. So the statement's "seven economies ... because each adopted a ban" is wrong.
4. **Incorrect.** USTR expressly declined to remove beef and avocados from the exemption list; they remained exempt. 91 FR 47331.
5. **Incorrect.** Japan and South Korea have net-of-MFN rates but no country-specific negotiated Annex II part; they are covered only by Part A. The EU, Switzerland and Taiwan have Parts C, D and K respectively. 91 FR 47324, 47327, 47327-28, 47395.
6. **Partly correct.** USTR added 471 products, but the text says "certain sugar and sugar containing products," not all sugar and sugar-containing products. 91 FR 47332.
7. **Incorrect.** The documents do not state that total duties will never exceed 12.5%. The 12.5% figure is the maximum section 301 additional rate; flat-rate economies pay it in addition to MFN. Only the net-rate economies are capped at a 10% or 12.5% total. 91 FR 47720; 91 FR 47320-21, 47334.
8. **Correct.** The notice states that covered goods admitted to a U.S. foreign trade zone, except those eligible for domestic status, may be admitted only as privileged foreign status. 91 FR 47321.
9. **Correct.** If an exemption is held invalid, the applicable tariff applies to imports to which the invalidated exemption applied. 91 FR 47335; 91 FR 47723.
10. **Correct.** Of the products proposed in Annex A, USTR exempted all except the non-pharmaceutical applications of certain chemical products, and it declined to remove beef, avocados, paprika, lithium hexafluorophosphate and forgings. 91 FR 47330-31.
Q14.uncertainty: Item 3 depends on how one counts the seven economies: the documents list six post-June ban adopters plus Jordan, but only four of those moved from 12.5% to 10%. The others were already at 10%.

Q15.answer:
The table gives the additional duties legally owed on each $100,000 entry. MFN is excluded. "N" = no USMCA claim; "U" = USMCA claim. 232 = section 232; IEEPA = northern-border IEEPA duty; 338 = section 338 motor-vehicle duty; 301 = forced-labor section 301 duty.

| Entry date | Case N | Case U | Why other duties are not owed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Feb. 10, 2025 | **$0** | **$0** | IEEPA was paused until Mar. 4, 2025 (EO 14197); Canada was still exempt from the aluminum section 232 tariff under Proclamation 9893 until Mar. 12, 2025; no 338 or 301 yet. |
| 2. Mar. 6, 2025 | IEEPA **$25,000**; 232 **$0**; total **$25,000** | IEEPA **$25,000**; 232 **$0**; total **$25,000** | IEEPA took effect Mar. 4. The USMCA exemption from IEEPA did not take effect until Mar. 7 (EO 14231). Canada's 232 exemption still ran until Mar. 12. No 338/301. |
| 3. Mar. 10, 2025 | IEEPA **$25,000**; 232 **$0**; total **$25,000** | **$0** | U is exempt from IEEPA under EO 14231 (effective Mar. 7); Canada's 232 exemption still ran until Mar. 12. N pays IEEPA only. |
| 4. Mar. 14, 2025 | IEEPA **$25,000**; 232 **$0**; total **$25,000** | 232 **$25,000**; IEEPA **$0**; total **$25,000** | Canada's 232 exemption ended Mar. 12. U is exempt from IEEPA but pays 232. N pays IEEPA; EO 14289 §3(a)(ii) bars stacking 232 on an IEEPA article. |
| 5. June 3, 2025 | IEEPA **$25,000**; 232 **$0**; total **$25,000** | 232 **$25,000**; IEEPA **$0**; total **$25,000** | The 50% 232 rate began June 4. N pays IEEPA only; U pays 232 only. No 338/301. |
| 6. June 10, 2025 | IEEPA **$25,000**; 232 **$0**; total **$25,000** | 232 **$50,000**; IEEPA **$0**; total **$50,000** | N pays IEEPA 25% instead of the 50% 232 rate because EO 14289 §3(a)(ii) forbids stacking. U pays the 50% 232 rate. |
| 7. Aug. 5, 2025 | IEEPA **$35,000**; 232 **$0**; total **$35,000** | 232 **$50,000**; IEEPA **$0**; total **$50,000** | EO 14325 raised the IEEPA rate to 35% effective Aug. 1. U remains exempt from IEEPA and pays 50% 232. |
| 8. Mar. 2, 2026 | 232 **$50,000**; total **$50,000** | 232 **$50,000**; total **$50,000** | IEEPA was terminated by EO 14389 (Feb. 20, 2026). The 10% temporary surcharge was in effect, but section 232 articles were excluded from it. No 338/301. |
| 9. June 10, 2026 | 232 **$50,000**; total **$50,000** | 232 **$50,000**; total **$50,000** | Same. The June 8 Annex I-C changes did not move these Annex I-A extrusions. Surcharge still excluded 232 goods. |
| 10. July 27, 2026 | 232 **$50,000**; total **$50,000** | 232 **$50,000**; total **$50,000** | Surcharge expired July 24. 338 not effective until Aug. 22. 301 effective July 24 but note 52(f)(1) exempts aluminum articles under 9903.82.02. |
| 11. Aug. 25, 2026 | 232 **$50,000**; 338 **$0**; total **$50,000** | same | 338 was effective Aug. 22 but the original motor-vehicle clause (2) excluded 232 articles. 301 exempt. |
| 12. Sept. 14, 2026 | 232 **$50,000**; 338 **$0**; total **$50,000** | same | Same; the Sept. 15 stacking change was not yet effective. |
| 13. Sept. 16, 2026 | 232 **$50,000** + 338 **$50,000**; total **$100,000** | same | The Sept. 15 motor-vehicle scope modification makes 338 apply in addition to 232. 301 exempt. |
| 14. Nov. 10, 2026 | 232 **$50,000** + 338 **$50,000**; total **$100,000** | same | Same; the Oct. 30 further modification did not remove these goods. 301 exempt. |

**Other duties then in force, and why not owed:**
- **IEEPA northern-border duty:** in force Mar. 4, 2025 through Feb. 20, 2026. On non-USMCA goods it applied instead of 232 because of EO 14289 §3(a)(ii); on USMCA goods it did not apply after Mar. 7, 2025. It ended before all 2026 dates.
- **Reciprocal IEEPA tariff (EO 14257):** did not stack with the northern-border IEEPA duty on non-USMCA goods, and USMCA goods were exempt; it was also terminated by EO 14389.
- **Temporary 10% import surcharge:** Feb. 24-July 24, 2026; it excluded section 232 articles and USMCA-duty-free Canadian goods, and had expired before Aug. 25, 2026.
- **Section 338 alcohol and dairy proclamations:** do not cover aluminum extrusions; the motor-vehicle proclamation does, but its 232 exclusion applied until Sept. 15, 2026.
- **Section 301:** Canada 10% from July 24, 2026, but note 52(f)(1) exempts aluminum articles entered under heading 9903.82.02.
